paragraphs: A young sannyasin went off to the forest and spent years meditating, worshipping and practising yoga. One day, as he sat under a tree, some dry leaves fell on his head. Looking up, he saw a crow and a crane fighting in the branches. Furious that they had dared to drop leaves on him, he glared at them, and a flash of fire shot from his head and burnt both birds to ashes. He was thrilled: he could now destroy with a single look.

Some time later he went into town to beg for food. At one door he called out for alms, and a woman's voice answered from inside, asking him to wait a little. He fumed silently: how dare she keep me waiting? She has no idea how powerful I am. Then the voice spoke again, telling him not to think so much of himself, because there was neither crow nor crane here. Stunned, he waited.

When she finally came out, he fell at her feet and asked how she had known. She said she was just an ordinary woman who knew nothing of yoga. She had kept him waiting because she was nursing her sick husband. All her life she had simply done her duty, first to her parents, then to her husband, and that had brought her enlightenment. If he wanted to learn more, she said, he should visit a Vyadha, a butcher, in a certain town's market.

The monk hesitated, but went. He found a big, heavy-set butcher hacking meat and haggling with customers, and was horrified. Yet the man looked up and asked whether the lady had sent him, and told him to sit until the day's work was done. At home, the butcher first bathed and fed his elderly parents, then turned to his guest. When the sannyasin asked about the soul and God, the butcher gave him a teaching that became part of the Mahabharata, the Vyadha-Gita, one of the loftiest expressions of Vedanta.

Amazed, the monk asked why someone so wise did such filthy, ugly work. The butcher's reply: 'No duty is ugly, no duty is impure.' Born into this trade, he did it well and without attachment, and cared for his parents. He had never practised yoga or left for the forest. All his wisdom had come from doing the duty of his own position, unattached.
learn: Spiritual greatness isn't measured by special powers or dramatic escapes; it shows up in how faithfully you do your everyday work. Respect every job and every person. Do your own role well, without ego, and growth will follow.
